title: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections)
hook: a brass pot polished before a festival doesn't get a new shine; the old one comes back, and Ramanuja says freedom works the same way

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vaishnava theology, Ramanuja's lamp: a self that's conscious by nature, its light narrowed in bondage and opened wide in freedom. When did your attention open a little wider? Day one thousand two hundred thirty.
screen: `THE LAMP AND ITS LIGHT.` · `TODAY: THE SHINE COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: The night before a festival, someone sits on the floor with the family's old brass pot, a lemon, some ash or tamarind, and a cloth. The pot has gone dull and brown. Rub, rinse, rub. And slowly it glows. Nobody added gold. Nothing new went in. The shine was the brass all along, under a film of time and smoke. Ramanuja reaches the last part of the Brahma Sutras, where the question is what happens to a self when it's finally free. Does it vanish? Does it turn into something else? His answer looks a lot like that pot on the floor.
screen: `THE OLD BRASS POT.` → `NOTHING NEW WENT IN.` → `WHAT HAPPENS WHEN A SELF IS FREE?`

segments.voice: The Chandogya Upanishad says the freed self, reaching the highest light, appears in its own form. The Brahma Sutra picks up that phrase, and Ramanuja leans hard on the word own. Freedom, he says, isn't the self getting a new nature. It's the self's real nature showing, the way the brass's shine shows. Its awareness, narrowed by karma, opens fully. It's free of evil, free of death and grief, with desires that come true, the same marks the Upanishad gave to the highest self. So does the freed self dissolve into God, like a drop into the sea? Not in Ramanuja's reading. The self stays a self. It knows Brahman directly, and experiences itself as inseparable from him, the way a body belongs to its soul. It shares Brahman's joy fully. But there's one line the Brahma Sutra draws, and Ramanuja keeps it. The freed self shares in everything except the running of the world. Creating, holding up and dissolving the universe stays with the Lord alone. Freed selves don't become rival gods. They're near enough to share every joy, and still themselves, still loving. That's the heart of it for Sri Vaishnavas: freedom isn't the end of the relationship. It's the relationship with nothing in the way. Other schools of Vedanta describe freedom differently, and each reads these same sutras with care.
screen: `IT APPEARS IN ITS OWN FORM.` · `NOTHING NEW, ONLY UNCOVERED.` · `STILL A SELF, NEVER APART.` · `EVERYTHING EXCEPT RUNNING THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: polish, don't add. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one good thing in you that's gone dull lately: patience, humor, generosity, attention. Don't try to make it new. Just picture the film over it, tiredness, hurry, an old hurt, and on each out-breath let a little of that film come away. Rub, rinse. Notice what was there all along. If you pray, you can hold that shine toward the name you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Vaishnava theology. Today, freedom as the self appearing in its own form: uncovered, still itself, near God, sharing every joy except running the world. Today's word.
Your line: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections). Today, let one good thing in you show again, without trying to become someone new. Day one thousand two hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas describe liberation, moksha, as the self reaching Vishnu's own realm, Vaikuntha, and serving him there forever in joy; teachers study Ramanuja's comments on the last section of the Brahma Sutras for this teaching.

pairs: nothing new, only the old shine

fork.setup: you're a freed self in Ramanuja's reading, sharing Brahman's joy completely. what don't you do?
fork.reveal: Ramanuja keeps the Brahma Sutra's line: freed selves share everything except the running of the world.

original.note: Sanskrit: in its own form, the Chandogya's phrase for the freed self, central to Ramanuja's reading.

trapdoor: what you thought: liberation means disappearing into God.
what it means: for Ramanuja, the self appears in its own form, still itself and never apart from God.
what a scholar hears: Brahma Sutra 4.4.1 on Chandogya 8.12.3, and 4.4.17's 'except world-business', read in the Sri Bhashya as equality in bliss, not in lordship.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.12.3 (reaching the highest light, it appears in its own form)
Brahma Sutra 4.4.1, 4.4.4 and 4.4.17, with Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya (own form; inseparable; except the running of the world)
Chandogya Upanishad 8.7.1 (free from evil, death and grief; whose desires are real)

notes: Ramanuja's comments on Brahma Sutra 4.4 are paraphrased; confirm especially 4.4.4 (experiencing itself as inseparable from Brahman) and 4.4.17 (jagadvyapara-varjam).
Applying the Chandogya 8.7.1 marks to the freed self follows Ramanuja's reading of 4.4.5; confirm.
The brass-polishing scene (lemon, ash or tamarind) is a household picture, not a source claim.
howItsDone mentions Vaikuntha and eternal service, which is standard Sri Vaishnava teaching but goes beyond the Sri Bhashya itself; confirm.
Devanagari स्वेन रूपेण and the stress in 'say' should be checked.
